lede: A pulse sent out and caught again tells you how far away something is. Ships find the seabed that way, hospitals find a baby, engineers find cracks inside steel. There is one number in it that has to be handled carefully.
can: Explain why a measured echo time covers twice the distance you want
Turn an echo time into a distance, and a known distance into a speed
Say what ultrasound is, and what sonar and radar each send out

md: Shout at a cliff and a moment later the cliff shouts back. A ship finds the seabed the same way, and a hospital scanner finds a baby. Each one sends out a pulse, waits, and times what comes back.

alt: A ship on the sea sends a sonar pulse straight down to the seabed, and the echo comes straight back up. The depth d is marked from the surface to the seabed.

caption: One pulse, two journeys: the timer runs from the moment the pulse leaves until its echo is back.

md: A pulse that comes back has made **two journeys**: out to whatever reflected it, and back again. The timer starts when the pulse leaves and stops when the echo arrives, so the time you are given always covers **both journeys**.

title: Why every echo has a factor of two
md: The pulse travels at one steady speed, down through the water and back up through the same water. So the two journeys take equal times, and each takes half of the measured time. Half the time means half the distance: every factor of two in this topic comes from that.

stem: A ship's echo sounder records 0.14 s between sending a pulse and receiving its echo from the seabed. How long did the pulse take to reach the seabed? [1]

steps.working: The timer ran from pulse to echo: 0.14 s.
steps.decision: Say first what the measured time covers: from the pulse leaving the ship to the echo arriving back.

steps.working: In that time the pulse went down to the seabed and came back up: two equal journeys.
steps.decision: The speed is the same on the way down and on the way up, so the two journeys take the same time.

steps.working: Time to reach the seabed = 0.14 ÷ 2 = 0.07 s
steps.decision: One journey is half of the there-and-back time.

prompt: A ship sends a sonar pulse straight down and times the echo. In the time its timer measures, how far does the pulse travel?
options: down to the seabed and back up again
half of the way down to the seabed
answer: down to the seabed and back up again
explain: The timer starts as the pulse leaves the ship and stops when the echo is back, so it covers the trip down and the trip back up, as step 2 of the See it shows. The answer: down to the seabed and back up again. Down to the seabed only is the depth, half of the path the timer covers.

optionNotes.why: It tempts because the depth is what you want, but the timer keeps running until the echo is back at the ship, so it also times the trip up.

optionNotes.option: half of the way down to the seabed
optionNotes.why: Halving is done to the distance after the calculation; the timer itself runs for the whole path, down and back.

twin.prompt: A bat calls and times the echo from a cave wall. In the time the bat measures, how far does its call travel?
options: to the wall and back again
half of the way to the wall
twin.answer: to the wall and back again
twin.explain: The bat's timing runs from its call to the echo, so the call goes out to the wall and returns. The answer: to the wall and back again. To the wall only is the one-way distance, half of the path.

text: 2. From an echo time to a distance

md: Use the speed equation you already know, v = d/t, turned round to d = v × t. With the whole measured time in it, v × t gives the **total** path, there and back. The distance to the reflector is **half** of that total.

title: The echo rule
md: **distance to the reflector = (speed × time) ÷ 2**. No physics equation is printed on the paper. The first mark is for a correct equation, so v = d/t written first earns it; the substitution, the total distance and the halved answer then earn a mark each.

stem: A climber claps at the mouth of a cave and hears the echo from the back wall 1.2 s later. Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. Calculate the distance to the back wall. [4]

figure.src: data:image/svg+xml;utf8,<svg viewBox="0 0 400 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><title>A timeline of one echo. The clap is at 0 s, the sound reaches the wall at 0.6 s and the echo is heard at 1.2 s: the first half of the time is the journey to the wall, the second half the journey back.</title><path d="M36 76 L186.8 76" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><path d="M194 76 L185.7 79.5 L185.7 72.5 Z" fill="currentColor"/><text x="115" y="62" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">to the wall</text><path d="M206 76 L356.8 76" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><path d="M364 76 L355.7 79.5 L355.7 72.5 Z" fill="currentColor"/><text x="285" y="62" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">back</text><path d="M30 108 L370 108" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><path d="M30 100 L30 116" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><path d="M200 100 L200 116" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><path d="M370 100 L370 116" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><text x="30" y="138" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor">0 s</text><text x="200" y="138" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">0.6 s</text><text x="370" y="138" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">1.2 s</text><text x="30" y="166" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor">clap</text><text x="200" y="166" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">at the wall</text><text x="370" y="166" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">echo heard</text></svg>
figure.alt: A timeline: the clap at 0 s, the sound at the wall at 0.6 s, the echo heard at 1.2 s.

steps.working: v = d/t, so d = v × t
steps.decision: Write the equation before any number. It earns the first mark, and a wrong equation scores nothing.
Put in the speed and the whole measured time.
This is the total path: the sound reached the wall and returned.
Halve it: the wall is one journey away. The answer must be smaller than the total.

prompt: A diver's sonar pulse returns from a wreck 0.024 s after it was sent. Sound travels at 1500 m/s in sea water. How far away is the wreck, in m?
explain: Speed × time gives the whole path out and back: 1500 × 0.024 = 36 m, as in step 3 of the See it. The wreck is one journey away, half of that: 18 m. If you wrote 36, that is the there-and-back total; halve it once.

twin.prompt: A shout echoes from a wall 0.7 s after it is made. Sound travels at 340 m/s in air. How far away is the wall, in m?
twin.explain: 340 × 0.7 = 238 m is the path there and back, so the wall is 238 ÷ 2 = 119 m away.

text: 3. From a known distance to a speed

md: Sometimes the paper gives the distance and asks for the speed. The factor of two now runs the other way: in the measured time the wave covered the distance **twice**, so **double the distance** before you divide by the time. Halving the time instead gives the same answer, and either route earns the marks.

stem: A student stands 99 m from a tall wall and claps once. The echo returns 0.6 s later. Calculate the speed of sound in the air. [4]

steps.decision: The equation first, as always.
The clap went to the wall and back, so the sound covered the 99 m twice.
Divide by the whole measured time: it matches the whole path.
The answer with its unit. Halving the time instead, 99 ÷ 0.3, gives the same 330 m/s.

prompt: A clap echoes back from a wall 34 m away, 0.2 s later. What is the speed of sound, in m/s?
explain: The sound covered 2 × 34 = 68 m in 0.2 s, as step 2 of the See it doubles the distance, so v = 68 ÷ 0.2 = 340 m/s. If you wrote 170, that divided the one-way 34 m by the there-and-back time; double the distance first.

twin.prompt: A sonar pulse returns from the seabed 45 m below a ship 0.06 s after it was sent. What is the speed of sound in the water, in m/s?
twin.explain: The pulse covered 2 × 45 = 90 m in 0.06 s, so the speed is 90 ÷ 0.06 = 1500 m/s.

text: 4. Ultrasound: sound too high to hear

alt: A frequency line, not to scale: sound a human ear can hear lies below 20 000 Hz, and sound above 20 000 Hz is ultrasound.

Sound a human ear can hear lies below 20 000 Hz; sound above 20 000 Hz is ultrasound.</title><path d="M20 96 L376.8 96" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><path d="M384 96 L375.7 99.5 L375.7 92.5 Z" fill="currentColor"/><path d="M230 88 L230 104" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><text x="230" y="126" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">20 000 Hz</text><path d="M24 62 L230 62" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/><path d="M24 56 L24 68" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/><path d="M230 56 L230 68" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none"/><text x="127" y="48" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle">a human ear hears</text><path d="M230 62 L380 62" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="306" y="48" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">ultrasound</text><text x="384" y="150" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">frequency, higher →</text></svg>
caption: Above 20 000 Hz a human ear hears nothing, but it is still sound: that is ultrasound.

md: **Ultrasound** is sound with a frequency greater than **20 000 Hz**, too high for a human ear. It is still sound, so it is **longitudinal** and needs particles to travel through. Keep it apart from **ultraviolet**, which is electromagnetic: the two words have been swapped in tables on more than one paper.

stem: An ultrasonic pest repeller gives out sound of frequency 28 kHz. Explain whether this sound is ultrasound. [2]

steps.decision: Kilo means a thousand: turn the frequency into hertz before you compare it.
Compare it with the threshold, the one number the definition carries.

steps.working: So it is ultrasound: sound too high for a human to hear.
steps.decision: Finish with the conclusion in the question's own words.

prompt: Ultrasound is sound with a frequency greater than ______ Hz.
explain: The threshold is the top of human hearing, 20 000 Hz, the number the pest repeller's 28 000 Hz was compared with in step 2 of the See it. The number is what earns the mark: very high-pitched on its own does not.

twin.prompt: Written in kilohertz, the lowest frequency of ultrasound is ______ kHz.
twin.explain: 20 000 Hz is 20 kHz, because one kilohertz is 1000 hertz.

alt: A probe on a metal block sends an ultrasound pulse down: echo 1 returns from a crack part way down, echo 2 later from the far face.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img"><title>A probe on top of a metal block sends an ultrasound pulse down. Part of it reflects from a crack part way down and returns first, echo 1; the rest reflects from the far face of the block and returns later, echo 2.</title><path d="M40 74 h320 v140 h-320 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.07"/><path d="M138 48 h56 v26 h-56 Z" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.2"/><text x="130" y="66" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">probe</text><path d="M120 128 L130 119 L140 130 L150 120 L160 131 L170 122" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2.4" fill="none"/><text x="114" y="134" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">crack</text><path d="M148 78 L148 110.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><path d="M148 118 L144.5 109.7 L151.5 109.7 Z" fill="currentColor"/><path d="M160 118 L160 85.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><path d="M160 78 L163.5 86.3 L156.5 86.3 Z" fill="currentColor"/><text x="144" y="108" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end">echo 1</text><path d="M176 78 L176 202.8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><path d="M176 210 L172.5 201.7 L179.5 201.7 Z" fill="currentColor"/><path d="M188 210 L188 85.2" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" fill="none"/><path d="M188 78 L191.5 86.3 L184.5 86.3 Z" fill="currentColor"/><text x="198" y="176" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor">echo 2</text><text x="44" y="238" font-family="inherit" font-size="15" fill="currentColor">far face</text></svg>
caption: One pulse, two echoes: the crack sends one back early, the far face sends one back later.

md: The specification names two uses of ultrasound. In **industry** it finds **defects in metals**; in **medicine** it measures the **head diameter of a foetus**. Both work the same way. A pulse reflects from **every boundary** it meets, so one pulse sends back several echoes. An **earlier echo means a nearer boundary**, and each time becomes a depth with the same halving.

alt: A grey and black ultrasound scan of a foetus in the womb, with two electronic caliper crosses placed on the screen, one at each end of the body, and the measured length printed beside them.
credit: Wolfgang Moroder, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
caption: A real scan. Every bright line in it is an echo, placed on the screen by the time it took to come back.
prompt: The sonographer puts two markers on the screen and the machine prints a length in millimetres. Explain how a machine that only measures times can print a length, and say what else it has to be told before it can.

stem: An ultrasound pulse is sent into a metal block. One echo returns after 0.00004 s and a second after 0.00012 s. Ultrasound travels at 5000 m/s in this metal. Find the depth of the crack and the thickness of the block. [4]

steps.working: First echo: 5000 × 0.00004 = 0.2 m there and back
steps.decision: The earlier echo comes from the nearer boundary, the crack.
Halve it, as for any echo.

steps.working: Second echo: 5000 × 0.00012 = 0.6 m there and back
steps.decision: The later echo comes from the far face of the block.
Halve again. The crack lies 0.1 m down inside a block 0.3 m thick.

title: GCSE Physics Revision "Ultrasound"
why: Freesciencelessons on what ultrasound is and how an echo time becomes a distance, beside our own worked steps.

prompt: Two echoes come back from one pulse sent into a steel block. What does the earlier one tell the engineer?
options: something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface
the block is made of two different metals
the pulse is travelling faster near the surface
answer: something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface
explain: An earlier echo has had a shorter journey, because the speed is the same all through the block: in the See it the first echo came back from the crack, only 0.1 m down. So the earlier echo means something is reflecting the pulse closer to the surface. No second metal or change of speed is needed.

optionNotes.option: the block is made of two different metals
optionNotes.why: A join between two metals would reflect too, but nothing in the reading says there is one; an earlier echo simply came from something nearer, such as a crack.

optionNotes.option: the pulse is travelling faster near the surface
optionNotes.why: A shorter time could come from a higher speed, but the speed is the same all through one block, so only a shorter journey explains the earlier echo.

twin.prompt: A scanner sends one ultrasound pulse into a patient and receives two echoes. Which echo came from the boundary nearer the probe?
options: the louder of the two echoes
twin.explain: Both echoes travel at the same speed, so the one with the shorter journey arrives first. The answer: the echo that arrived first. Loudness does not tell you the distance.

md: **Sonar** sends **pulses of sound** through water, to find the seabed, a shoal of fish or a wreck. **Radar** sends pulses of **electromagnetic waves**, radio waves or microwaves, through the air, to find **aircraft and ships**. Radar pulses travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s, so an echo from an aircraft tens of kilometres away is back in less than a thousandth of a second.

stem: (a) A trawler must find a shoal of fish under the water. Say whether it should use sonar or radar, and give a reason. [2] (b) An airport's radar echo from an aircraft returns 0.00012 s after the pulse is sent. Radio waves travel at 3 × 10⁸ m/s. Calculate the distance to the aircraft in km. [4]

steps.working: (a) Sonar: the shoal is under water, and sonar sends pulses of sound through water.
steps.decision: Under water it is sonar, and sonar is sound; radar is for aircraft and ships.
Radar is electromagnetic, so its pulse travels at 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
On a calculator, type 3 × 10⁸ as 3E8. This is the path out to the aircraft and back.

steps.working: Distance to the aircraft = 36 000 ÷ 2 = 18 000 m = 18 km
steps.decision: Halve for one journey, then divide by 1000 for kilometres.

prompt: A lifeboat crew must find a sunken boat on the seabed and also track a helicopter above the sea. Which pairing is right?
options: seabed: sonar, sending sound pulses; helicopter: radar, sending electromagnetic waves
seabed: radar, sending electromagnetic waves; helicopter: sonar, sending sound pulses
seabed: sonar, sending electromagnetic waves; helicopter: radar, sending sound pulses
answer: seabed: sonar, sending sound pulses; helicopter: radar, sending electromagnetic waves
explain: Under water the system is sonar, and sonar sends sound (step 1 of the See it); through the air to an aircraft it is radar, which sends electromagnetic waves (step 2). So the seabed takes sonar with sound pulses and the helicopter radar with electromagnetic waves. Swapping either the systems or the waves loses the mark.

optionNotes.option: seabed: radar, sending electromagnetic waves; helicopter: sonar, sending sound pulses
optionNotes.why: This swaps the two systems: radar is for aircraft and ships, and sonar is for objects under the water.

optionNotes.option: seabed: sonar, sending electromagnetic waves; helicopter: radar, sending sound pulses
optionNotes.why: The systems are right but the waves are swapped: sonar sends pulses of sound, and radar sends electromagnetic waves.

twin.prompt: A harbour tracks a ship arriving on the surface while divers map a wreck below it. Which pairing is right?
options: ship: radar, sending electromagnetic waves; wreck: sonar, sending sound pulses
ship: sonar, sending sound pulses; wreck: radar, sending electromagnetic waves
ship: radar, sending sound pulses; wreck: sonar, sending electromagnetic waves
twin.answer: ship: radar, sending electromagnetic waves; wreck: sonar, sending sound pulses
twin.explain: Ships and aircraft are found by radar, which sends electromagnetic waves; anything under water is found by sonar, which sends sound. So the ship takes radar and the wreck sonar.

md: **Distance given, speed wanted.** The stem gives the distance to a wall and the time to the wall and back, then asks for the speed (Summer 2024 Higher). Double the distance, or halve the time, before you divide.

**A frequency in kilohertz.** The wave equation turns up inside an ultrasound question with the frequency in kHz (Summer 2025 Higher) or in standard form (Summer 2024 Higher). Change it to hertz first: that conversion earns a mark of its own.

**Ultrasound or ultraviolet?** A table of waves to sort (Summer 2023 and 2025 Foundation) is lost on one word. Ultrasound is sound, so it goes with the longitudinal waves. Ultraviolet is electromagnetic, so it goes with the transverse waves.

stem: A bat's call has a frequency of 68 kHz and travels at 340 m/s in air. Calculate its wavelength. [4]

steps.decision: The wave equation. Recall it: the paper does not print it.
Convert before you substitute: kilo is a thousand, and the conversion earns its own mark.
Substitute the speed and the frequency in hertz.
Rearrange and finish with the unit: 5 mm, sensibly short for ultrasound.

prompt: An ultrasound probe works at 25 kHz in water, where sound travels at 1500 m/s. What is the wavelength, in m?
explain: Convert first: 25 kHz is 25 000 Hz, as in step 2 of the See it. Then λ = v ÷ f = 1500 ÷ 25 000 = 0.06 m. If you wrote 60, the kilo was left out, which makes the wavelength a thousand times too long.

twin.prompt: A parking sensor on a car sends ultrasound of frequency 55 kHz through air, where sound travels at 330 m/s. What is the wavelength, in m?

md:
Explain why an echo time covers the distance twice, there and back.
Halve the total for a distance: distance = (speed × time) ÷ 2.
Double the distance, or halve the time, when a speed is wanted.
State that ultrasound is sound above 20 000 Hz, with its medical and industrial use.
Pair sonar with sound pulses and radar with electromagnetic waves.

An echo calculation is worth [3] or [4]: a correct equation first, then the substitution, the total distance and the halved answer, a mark each; a wrong equation scores nothing. In an ultrasound question the kilohertz conversion earns its own mark, and the definition and each use are [1]. Stuck? Draw the there-and-back arrows and ask whether you want a distance (halve) or a speed (double).
